body: As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital services grows, opposition to new data center development is growing with it. In many communities, critics are trying to define these projects before the broader public has a chance to weigh the full picture. That’s a mistake.
For small businesses,
data centers are
not a distant tech matter. They are
part of critical infrastructure driving the platforms and services that shape how small businesses compete, grow, and innovate

in the digital economy. SBE Council’s research shows that among the 82% of small business employers using AI, for example, 93% expect to keep investing in it over the next year, 81% say AI tools are vital to their competitiveness
, and 82% believe winning the global AI race is essential to the future of the U.S. economy.

The same research shows the vast percentage of small businesses are using a wide array of digital platforms and tools. The fact that most small businesses have embedded AI and digital tools into their day-to-day operations makes the need for data centers more than a debate about land use or utility demand. It is about whether the United States will support the infrastructure that small businesses and entrepreneurs increasingly depend on to compete and grow their firms.

A fact-based discussion should absolutely take concerns seriously. But it should also flesh out the broad claims pushed by national politicians, opportunistic political candidates, and local activists where fear-based tactics are being deployed. Three of the most common myths deserve more balanced discussion.
Myth 1: Data centers do not create enough jobs or economic activity to justify the investment.
Facts: This argument usually focuses only on the permanent staffing levels inside a completed facility. That leaves out a large share of the economic activity data centers generate.

A 2025 PwC report commissioned by the Data Center Coalition found that each direct data center job supports more than six jobs elsewhere in the U.S. economy, while the industry’s total annual employment contribution reached 4.7 million jobs

in 2023. A report from the Virginia legislature’s policy analysis arm, JLARC, also found that construction is a major source of employment impact, with a single building often supporting about 1,500 workers on site at peak activity. That matters because the opportunity extends well beyond the walls of the facility itself. Data center development supports contractors and a range of other local service providers – small businesses – that help bring projects online and keep them running. For communities trying to broaden their economic base, that is meaningful activity. It is fair to ask whether a project is well-structured and well-sited. It is not fair to suggest the benefits stop with a handful of technicians.
Myth 2: Data centers are an unnecessary burden on the gri
d.
Facts: Data centers do use significant electricity and communities are right to expect serious grid planning. But opponents often present power demand as though it is the end of the story.
In reality, rising data center load is one reason utilities and policymakers are accelerating conversations about grid modernization and long-term capacity planning.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported in March 2026 that data centers are a key driver of electricity demand growth, while PwC has noted that large customers are increasingly tied to broader infrastructure planning and new approaches to managing load. The more useful question is not whether data centers consume electricity. Of course they do. The question is whether policymakers are shaping development in ways that strengthen and modernize the system to support broader economic growth. If communities want better outcomes, the answer is smart planning and accountability, not the false claim that digital infrastructure offers no value beyond its power bill.
Moreover, tech companies are exploring and pursuing a myriad of options to bring their own power (BYOP)
. Policies and elected officials need to support reasonable initiatives to enable such investment and innovative solutions.
Myth 3: Data centers are a poor use of land because they are just big buildings with little broader community value.

Facts: This criticism tends to focus on appearance rather than function. Data centers may not look like the type of development some activists prefer, but that does not make them low-value assets. They are part of the physical backbone of the digital economy. Virginia’s JLARC found that data centers can generate substantial state and local tax revenue through real estate and business personal property taxes. The Northern Virginia Technology Council similarly reported that Virginia data centers drive billions in statewide economic impact and major annual tax contributions. That revenue matters to local communities. It can help fund public priorities and expand fiscal capacity in places that want to invest in long-term growth. None of this means every proposal belongs everywhere. Community fit still matters. But the sweeping claim that data centers are inherently a bad use of land is overly broad and inappropriate for many areas.
Conclusion

The backlash against data centers is gaining momentum in some places because opponents have been effective at reducing a complex issue to a simple political target. But the small business economy deserves a fuller, fact-based conversation. SBE Council has already made clear that fear-based policymaking is the wrong approach when it comes to AI and the infrastructure supporting these tools. That same principle applies here.

Data centers support a growing small business ecosystem, strengthen local economies, and help sustain the technologies entrepreneurs are already using to compete. The right path is not blanket opposition. It is smart siting, clear standards, and a fact-based understanding of what responsible digital infrastructure can mean for American communities, entrepreneurship, and small business growth.
